I cannot continue to exist in this bungalow as a ghost while the rightful tenant stands before me in polite confusion. I will ask him to join me for a moment of conversation to clarify our respective positions, for the state must not be a house of errors.

It is time to read what the retired IAS officer has written; he knows the occupant, and his knowledge is the key to unlocking my own standing here.

Shri Malhotra’s letter lies in the study, a correspondence from a retired IAS officer who knows who I am, or rather, who I am supposed to be. Ramesh has secured the silence I require. The Malhotra letter is not merely a bureaucratic error; it is a question of who I am to this state, and whether the accident of my residence here is to be treated as a fact or an anomaly. I must read it now, before the afternoon heat settles and the mind grows heavy.
Thank you, Ramesh. You may withdraw.
Ji sir, you need anything else, just ring the bell.

I will sit with him for a moment; the caretaker is the first link in the ethical substance of the household.
Thank you, Ramesh. The samosas are a welcome respite. Sit, please.
No, sir. You should eat while they are warm. I will just be in the kitchen if you need anything else.

The samosas are a small concession to the body, but the mind is already turning to the Malhotra letter. A retired IAS officer who 'knows the occupant' is a thread that must be pulled before it tangles with the Directorate's error. I will not waste the evening; the study is waiting.
Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

The parakeets descend on the tree in a sudden, loud exodus, a spectacle of nature that mocks the silence of the house. I have missed my afternoon errand and the mind is restless, but the body is satiated from the samosas. It is nearly six o'clock; the light is fading, and the German lesson for Ananya is at five, which I must have either forgotten or the schedule has shifted. I cannot walk now in the gathering dark without a purpose, and I have not yet read Malhotra's letter.

The evening settles in, and the parakeets have finally ceased their noisy exodus. Ramesh stands before me, and I am not yet ready to discuss the electricity bill or the Malhotra letter; the mind needs a quiet interval to arrange itself. I shall let him know that I am resting before dinner.
Ramesh, please leave me be for a moment. I am resting my eyes before dinner.
Ji sir. I will be in the kitchen. You rest your eyes.

Ramesh withdraws with a nod, leaving Hegde and me in the drawing room. The man who was meant to be me sits across the table, a ghost of the correct name, while I am the error that was left behind. The Malhotra letter remains the pressing matter; the state’s paperwork is a matter of duty, however confused the identity.

Dinner arrives: rotis, dal makhani, and curd. Hegde is present, a living proof that my identity is a clerical error, which shakes the notion of the self as a stable substance. I will eat, for the body requires its own logic, and then I must address the matter of the state and its mistaken occupant.

Shri Hegde, you are the Joint Secretary, I am the philosopher, and yet here we are, sharing a table in a house that belongs to neither of us by right, but by the accident of a misplaced initial. The state, it seems, is not the actuality of the ethical idea, but a filing system that occasionally misfiles its own souls.
Sir, with respect, I’m here to eat and sign the register, not to debate dialectics. Please, try the dal makhani before it gets cold.

Dear Dr. Lindner,

The fog in Munich is a thing of the imagination, I suspect, whereas the dust here is a thing of the body. It settles in the creases of the kurta, in the hair, and in the joints. I am writing to you from the same brown suspension, though the air today is clearer, a dry 23 degrees that sharpens the mind if it does not comfort it. You asked me to keep writing, and I have. Not to the Directorate, though that correspondence continues its slow, grinding march, but to myself, in the quiet of the afternoon.

I have been rereading the *Iliad* in the margin of my days. You are right that it is appropriate. Achilles is not a man who waits for the universal to resolve his confusion; he is a man who is displaced by a system—Agamemnon’s honor, the Greek assembly, the gods—that claims to be rational but acts on caprice. My displacement is different in kind, but the same in structure. I am a particular that the universal (the Directorate) cannot sublate. I am not a guest, nor am I the allottee. I am a remainder. The *Iliad* teaches us that the hero’s anger is not a failure of reason, but the excess of reason that the system cannot contain. I find myself in that excess. I am angry, not at the error, but at the silence that follows it. The state does not speak; it processes. And in that processing, I am erased.

Ramesh, my caretaker, has begun to treat me with a kind of wary respect. He brings the chai, he sweeps the veranda, he does not ask questions. He is, as you say, a practical man. Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

You ask how I fare in this strange new chapter. I wake each day in a bungalow that belongs, on paper, to a Mr. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. My file is currently “gone up for orders,” and I am told to wait fifteen days. In the meantime, I am a ghost in the machine, a particular will suspended between the universal claim of the administration and the immediate necessity of my own body.

The air today is hazy, the index standing at 150, a brown suspension that chokes the sky. Instead, I sat in the study, watching the dust motes dance in the light, and I found myself reconsidering my earlier lectures on the East. I had spoken of a spirit that dreams, fixed in nature, lacking the self-consciousness to build a state of its own making. But here, in the dust and the haze, I see a different movement. The rain has stopped, but the cold has set in. I am keeping a bottle of warm wine by the fire, a small comfort against the grey.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner
